newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Pension fund wins stake in Russian Surgut oil.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Pension fund wins stake in Russian Surgut oil.

text.p: A little-known pension fund won a 40 percent stake in Surgut Holding, one of Russia's top three oil companies, on Tuesday.
But share dealers and oil analysts said the move, which effectively consolidates management control over the group, came as no surprise.
Surgut Holding (NK Surgutneftegaz) said pension-fund manager ZAO Surgutfondinvest had won an investment tender for 40.12 percent of Surgut Holding.
The state-owned stake had been held in trust on behalf of the government by Surgut Holding's pension fund, which in turn is mostly owned by Surgut Holding.
Surgut officials declined to say whether the two pension funds were related.
But analysts said the terms of the tender had made it virtually possible for an investor outside the Surgut group to win the stake.
"It's basically the Surgut pension fund mark two," said Stephen O'Sullivan, oil and gas director at MC Securities in London.
"If it's a Surgut structure then it's positive. It's what was expected," said Salomon Bros analyst Elena Merkoulova.
"It means that the privatisation and the strategy that Surgut envisaged for the holding company and the (production company) will go at their own pace," she said.
Surgutfondinvest paid 415 billion roubles ($73 million) for the four million shares, barely above the starting price of 410 billion. Only one other, unnamed, bidder took part in the tender.
The winner of the tender must transfer five percent of Surgut Holding's main operating company, AO Surgutneftegaz to Surgut Holding, making it all but impossible for an outsider to win.
Surgut Holding, one of a dozen Russian vertically integrated oil groups created in the last few years, currently owns 38 percent of Surgutneftegaz, including 51 percent of the voting shares.

Surgutneftegaz has performed strongly in the current Russian share rally, boosted by an issue of American Depositary Shares (ADRs). It eased to $0.750 on Tuesday from $0.753 on Monday in a generally weaker market.
O'Sullivan of MC Securities forecast that Surgut Holding, whose shares are not widely traded, would now consolidate its shares with Surgutneftegaz to create a single stock.
Although management resented outside interference, it was proving more responsive to investors, as the ADR issue and plans for ADRs on preferred stock showed, he said.
The winner of the tender must also transfer 1.2 trillion roubles to Surgut Holding for investment within three months.

Surgut's pension fund won the stake in Surgut Holding in November 1995 in the first transaction under a controversial shares-for-loans programme, in which investors won the right to manage state-owned shares in partly privatised companies in return for loans to the government.

Tuesday's tender was the third sale of stakes acquired in shares-for-loans deals, after auctions of stakes in oil groups YUKOS and SIDANKO. In both these cases the auctions were won by bidders apparently close to the winners of the original shares-for-loans contests.
But the result of those deals was to give control of YUKOS and SIDANKO to two of the major banks, Menatep and Uneximbank, which had promoted the sales-for-loans scheme.
Surgut Holding emerged from the tender with no bank in control, and analysts said this was positive.
Shareholders may have to wait many years to see the benefits of corporate restructuring by Menatep at the YUKOS group, said Salomon's Markoulova.
"I'm much more comfortable seeing the company running its own operations," said Salomon's Merkoulova.
